posts.title: What We Talk About When We Talk About Our Characters
posts.description: You hear that creaking? No, it’s not a bundle of winter-dry branches straining against a chilling wind or chestnuts popping as they roast on a fire. That’s my back and those are my knees. Because folks, I’m old, and this next sentence will cement that fact: back in my day, talking to someone, unprompted, about your D&D character was the height of cringe. And sure, cornering Linda at the office holiday party to yap nonstop about a bundle of numbers and stats divorced from any sort of context is still pretty cringe, but does that mean we shouldn’t do it? Well, yes. Please do not isolate someone and drone on in a one-way conversation for twenty minutes. But no, talking about our characters should be encouraged. We put our hearts into these blorbos. We send’em through hell both emotional and literal (well, fictionally literal). They’re important to us, and we should share that with people we care about. posts.title: Preparing for a New Game
posts.description: After nearly 18 months, my Blades In The Dark game is coming to a close. Our table selected Xcrawl Classics as our next game. While I love learning and playing new games, as someone who is neurodivergent, I hate giving up my established systems for how I run my game. Not only do I need to learn a new set of rules and setting, but I also have to build a new workflow for prep and campaign management, as well as templates for my prep. I’ll walk you through how I work through this process. It starts by understanding the three areas of consideration for any game… What The Game Needs Before we go through the process, we need to recognize that each game has certain things it needs in order to prep, run, and manage the game. Some games will need battlemats and tokens, others will need the management of decks of cards, some will have dice, some will need reference tables.
